sealLevels.name: No Sovereignty
sealLevels.description: No sovereign control; fully dependent on a foreign-controlled provider.

sealLevels.name: Jurisdictional Sovereignty
sealLevels.description: Operated under EU jurisdiction, but control can still be overridden from outside.

sealLevels.name: Data Sovereignty
sealLevels.description: The EU controls the data even under stress; outside parties cannot compel access.

sealLevels.name: Technological Sovereignty
sealLevels.description: The EU controls the technology and can keep operating if a foreign supplier withdraws.

sealLevels.name: Full Digital Sovereignty
sealLevels.description: Complete sovereign control across law, data, and technology, down to the supply chain.

roles.name: Architecture
roles.description: Designs the estate; owns topology and platform choices.

roles.name: Platform ops
roles.description: Runs the estate day to day.

roles.name: Security
roles.description: Owns controls, identity, and incident response.

roles.name: Legal
roles.description: Owns contracts, jurisdiction, and data-protection law.

roles.name: Procurement
roles.description: Owns supplier selection, exit, and commercial terms.

roles.name: Facilities/ESG
roles.description: Owns data-centre siting, power, and sustainability.

parties.name: Institution
parties.description: The assessed party — the estate owner (EC: Contracting Authority).

parties.name: Subprocessor
parties.description: A legal entity involved in delivery of the contract.

questions.text: Under which jurisdiction's law can the primary provider be compelled to disclose or hand over your data?
questions.why: If a foreign court can compel disclosure, no amount of encryption restores control — this is the kill-switch on legal sovereignty.

ladder.description: A non-EU jurisdiction (e.g. under the US CLOUD Act) can compel disclosure directly from the provider.
Only EU/EEA jurisdiction applies; no foreign government can lawfully compel the provider.
EU jurisdiction applies and the provider is contractually and technically unable to comply with a foreign disclosure order.

questions.text: Who ultimately owns and controls the primary provider's parent company?
questions.why: Ownership decides who can be pressured by a foreign state; an EU-operated subsidiary is only as sovereign as its parent allows.

ladder.description: Controlled by a non-EU parent subject to foreign extraterritorial law.
A non-EU parent exists but an EU entity holds operational control under a trust or ring-fencing arrangement.
No non-EU parent; ownership and control sit wholly within the EU/EEA.

questions.text: If the provider were compelled by a foreign authority to suspend your service, could you keep operating?
questions.why: Capability-under-stress: sovereignty is what still works when access breaks, not how well the programme runs on a good day.

ladder.description: Service would stop; there is no alternative and no exit plan.
A documented exit plan exists but has never been exercised; recovery would take months.
Workloads and data are portable to an EU-controlled alternative within days, tested at least once.
An EU-controlled alternative runs in parallel; a cut-off is survivable with no loss of service.

questions.text: Are the physical data-centre facilities (power, cooling, building access) run by an operator you can name and hold to EU jurisdiction?
questions.why: Facilities sit beneath every other control; a foreign-operated building is a real gap the software layer cannot close — recorded as context, it informs the picture but does not by itself set the floor.

ladder.description: Facilities are run by a non-EU party under non-EU control; the operator is not fully known.
An EU-based operator runs the facilities under EU jurisdiction, with some dependence on non-EU maintenance or parts.
Facilities are wholly EU-operated and EU-controlled end to end, including maintenance and physical access.

questions.text: For this technical dimension, who controls the technology, and could you keep operating if a foreign supplier withdrew support?
questions.why: Capability-under-stress, per dimension: a dimension is only as sovereign as its ability to run without a supplier who can be compelled from outside the EU.

ladder.description: Wholly dependent on a foreign-controlled supplier; no EU-controlled alternative exists.
Foreign-controlled today, but an EU-jurisdiction contract governs the relationship.
An EU-controlled alternative exists and data stays under EU control, though the supplier is not yet EU-controlled.
EU-controlled technology; operation continues if the foreign supplier withdraws.
Fully EU-controlled end to end, including the supply chain beneath this dimension.
